title: How big is Mars's giant volcano?

hook.banner: How big is Mars's biggest volcano?

narration.heading: Mars
narration.text: You think Everest is tall? Wait till you stand on Mars.

narration.heading: Olympus Mons
narration.text: This is Olympus Mons, roughly tied for the tallest mountain in the whole solar system.

narration.heading: 2.5 Everests
narration.text: It's about two and a half times as tall as Everest, and six hundred kilometres wide.

narration.heading: Size of Italy
narration.text: Its base covers an area about the size of Italy. At the top, six craters sit nested together.

narration.heading: Valles Marineris
narration.text: Spin around to Valles Marineris, a canyon more than four thousand kilometres long and up to seven kilometres deep.

narration.heading: Hellas
narration.text: And Hellas, an impact basin over two thousand kilometres wide, punched out by a giant asteroid billions of years ago.

narration.heading: Thicker air
narration.text: Its floor is so deep, the air down there is about twice as thick as the Martian average.

narration.heading: The twist
narration.text: The twist? Stand on top of Olympus Mons, and you wouldn't even know you're on a mountain.

narration.heading: Over the horizon
narration.text: Its slopes are so gentle, they run far beyond the horizon, just three kilometres away. Would you climb it?

skit.text: A mountain you can't see from the top? Like my to-do list.

titles: What if you stood on top of Mars's giant volcano?
Olympus Mons: the mountain so big you can't see it
youtube.description: A spin around Mars from Olympus Mons, two and a half times taller than Everest, to the Valles Marineris canyon and the Hellas impact basin, and why you wouldn't know you were on a mountain at its top.

sources.claim: Olympus Mons is roughly tied with Rheasilvia as the tallest known mountain in the Solar System; about 21.9 km high, about 2.5 times Everest's elevation; 600 km wide; about 300,000 km², roughly the size of Italy; six nested summit calderas 60 × 80 km; average slope about 5%; the slope runs far beyond the horizon, about 3 km away; at 18.65° N, 226.2° E
Valles Marineris is more than 4,000 km long and up to 7 km deep, at 13.9° S, 59.2° W

Hellas Planitia is about 2,300 km across, its floor about 7,152 m below the Martian datum, with air pressure about 103% higher than at the datum; it formed in an impact about 4.1–3.8 billion years ago; at 42.4° S, 70.5° E
